Evaluation Strategy for Term - End Project of Undergraduate Students, BS 
DYOD, IUST Awantipora  
1. Objective    
The primary objective of this evaluation strategy is to provide a structured and systematic approach for 
assessing undergraduate student projects  across various phases. This ensures consistency, fairness, and 
thoroughness in the assessment process, promoting a comprehensive evaluation of the   students' work.  
2. Evaluation Framework    
The evaluation process is structured around four key phases: Projec t Proposal, Project Implementation, 
Project Testing and Evaluation , and Project Documentation & Mentor Evaluation. Each phase will be 
assessed using specific criteria outlined in the provided rubric, ensuring clarity and   objectivity in the 
evaluation.  
3. P hase Breakdown     
Phase 1: Project Proposal (10 Points)  
Clarity (2.5 Points):    
Assessment Method: Evaluate the clarity of the proposal in articulating objectives and goals.    
Criteria: Clear and precise expression of project aims and measurable outcomes.    
Relevance and Importance (2.5 Points):    
Assessment Method: Review the justification for the project's relevance to the field.    
Criteria: Demonstrated significance and potential impact within the discipline.    
Feasibility (2.5 Points):    
Assessment Metho d: Analyze the realism of the project's resource assessment, timeline, and anticipated 
challenges.    
Criteria: Practical and achievable planning, considering availab le resources and constraints.    
Innovation (2.5 Points):    
Assessment Method: Assess the or iginality and creativity of the approach.    
Criteria: Novelty in approach, research me thods, or solution development.  
Phase 2: Project Implementation (40 Points)  
Literature Study (5 Points):    
Assessment Method: Evaluate the comprehensiveness and relevance of the literature review and theoretical 
framework.    
Criteria: A thorough review of relevant literature and a clear understanding of existing methods   and 
technologies in the field.

Rationale for Evaluation Framework  
Phase 1: Project Proposal (10 Po ints)    
The project proposal establishes the foundation for the entire project. By evaluating clarity, feasibility, 
relevance, and innovation, this phase ensures that students have properly conceptualized their project. A 
strong proposal provides direction , ensuring that students begin their work with clear and achievable goals.  
Phase 2: Project Implementation (40 Points)    
This phase is critical as it evaluates the execution of the project, including technical skills, problem - solvin g 
abilities, and  resource management. It is the most weighted phase because it reflects students' ability to appl y 
their knowledge and skills to real - world challenges, promoting practical learning.  
Phase 3: End - Term Presentation (30 Points)    
The presentation phase assesse s students' ability to communicate effectively, a critical skill in academia and  
the professional world. It evaluates how well students convey their project objectives, methods, and findings,  
ensuring that students can present their work in a clear, cohere nt, and professional manner.  
Phase 4: Project Documentation and Mentor Evaluation (20 Points)    
The documentation phase evaluates how well students reflect on their work and the rigor with which they 
document their process. It also allows mentors to assess   students' growth, consistency, and professionalism. 
This phase highlights the importance of accountability and professional communication in both academic and 
career contexts.  
 
Important Notes:    
1. Mentor Presence at Presentations: No presentation will b e entertained without the presence of the 
project mentor. The mentor must be present during the presentation to validate the project ’ s 
execution and to ensure the authenticity of the student ’ s work.    
2. Progress Submission: Progress at each stage of the p roject must be submitted to the office, and it 
should be vetted and signed off by the mentor.    
3. Project Timeline: The project timeline must be submitted in advance and be approved by the 
mentor. It should reflect a realistic and achievable schedule, wit h all milestones and deadlines 
clearly outlined and aligned with the project ’ s objectives.

37.documentTitle: From Waste Paper to Seed Paper Phase 2: Detailed Project Implementation & Methodology
37.subject: Sustainability & Material Reuse
37.heading: FROM WASTE PAPER TO SEED
37.text:
FROM WASTE PAPER TO SEED
PAPER
PHASE 2: DETAILED PROJECT IMPLEMENTATION &
METHODOLOGY
Team Members:  Sadiya, Gufran, Aatif
Affiliation:  Design Your Own Degree (DYOD), IUST Awantipora
1. Project Background & Objectives
Large amounts of paper are discarded daily across the Islamic University of Science and Technology
(IUST) campus. A significant portion of this paper, used for assignments, tests, and packaging, is
thrown away after a single use. While conventional recycling gives paper another temporary use, it
eventually becomes waste again. Our project aims to address this issue by transforming university
paper waste into a useful, biodegradable product: seed paper.
By integrating viable seeds into handmade recycled paper, we change the paper from something that
is simply discarded into something that can have a second, life-giving purpose. This document
outlines the step-by-step physical process we are executing to collect, process, and manufacture our
prototype seed paper using practical, hands-on methods.
2. Phase A: Gathering and Preparation
Phase 2 Implementation Report: Waste Paper to Seed Paper Page 1 of 6

38.documentTitle: From Waste Paper to Seed Paper Phase 2: Detailed Project Implementation & Methodology
38.subject: Sustainability & Material Reuse
38.heading: Step 1: Collection from IUST Campus
38.text:
Step 1: Collection from IUST Campus
The first step in our methodology was to find suitable
raw material. We walked around the IUST campus and
systematically  visited  different  locations,  including
academic classrooms, offices, and the student hostels.
We gathered a wide variety of discarded paper that
would otherwise end up in the trash. This diverse mix
included thrown-away test papers with handwriting, old
crumpled  lecture  notes,  and  leftover  corrugated
cardboard packaging. Sourcing our material directly
from the campus ensures our project directly addresses
local university waste. Fig 1: Discarded test paper collected
from classrooms.
Step 2: Cleaning and Purifying the Waste
Before the paper could be turned into new pulp, it had
to  be  completely  cleaned.  We  meticulously  went
through  all  the  collected  materials  by  hand.  We
carefully removed all staples, metal paper clips, plastic
tape,  and  laminated  pieces.  This  is  a  crucial
environmental step; if plastic and metal are left in the
mix, they not only ruin the soft paper pulp and damage
the  blending  equipment,  but  they  also  introduce
harmful microplastics into the soil when the seed paper
is eventually planted. Fig 2: Crumpled paper being checked

39.heading: Step 3: Sorting by Paper Type
39.text:
Step 3: Sorting by Paper Type
Not all paper breaks down the same way. We sorted our
clean waste into different categories based on their
thickness, fiber quality, and ink content. We created
separate  piles  for  rough  brown  cardboard  waste,
ordinary white A4 paper, and heavily printed test
papers. Sorting allows us to control the color and
physical strength of the final seed paper. We anticipate
that cardboard fibers will yield thicker, sturdier paper,
while standard A4 notes will result in a finer, smoother
texture.
Fig 3: Corrugated cardboard waste
sorted by fiber type.
Step 4: Cutting and Tearing
Large, intact pieces of paper take a very long time to
absorb water. To speed up the soaking process, we used
scissors and our hands to cut and tear the sorted paper
into small strips and tiny fragments. Tearing the paper
by hand is highly effective because it creates frayed,
feathered edges on the fibers, which bind together much
better during the final sheet formation process than
sharp scissor cuts. The smaller the pieces, the larger the
surface area exposed to water. Fig 4: Clean white paper cut into strips
for maximum surface area.

40.heading: 3. Phase B: Pulping and Sheet Formation
40.text:
3. Phase B: Pulping and Sheet Formation
Step 5: Hydration and Soaking
We placed all our prepared paper fragments into a large
bucket and filled it with water until the material was
completely submerged. We allow the paper to soak for
an extended period (typically 12 to 24 hours). This deep
hydration is essential; the water penetrates and softens
the tough cellulose fibers within the paper, naturally
breaking down their structure so they can be reshaped
into fresh sheets.
画
FIBER SOAKING
PROCESS
Fig 5: Softening the cellulose fibers.
Step 6: Blending into Pulp Slurry
Once the paper is mushy, we take handfuls of the wet
mass and place them into a blender. We add plenty of
fresh water to the blender to ensure the motor doesn't
overheat or jam. Using short, controlled pulses, we
blend the mixture until the mechanical action separates
the fibers completely. The result is a thick, smooth, and
cloudy liquid known as a "pulp slurry," which is the
foundational material for our new paper.

MECHANICAL
PULPING
Fig 6: Creating the pulp slurry.
Step 7: Engineering a Homemade Mesh
In traditional paper making, a tool called a "mould and
deckle" is used to lift pulp from the water. To maintain
sustainability  and  low  costs,  we  engineered  one
ourselves.  We  lashed  four  straight  wooden  sticks
together securely to form a rigid square frame. We then
stretched a piece of thin, porous mesh cloth tightly
across the wooden frame, securing it firmly so it
provides a flat, strong surface for the paper to settle on.

DIY MOULD
& DECKLE
Fig 7: Constructing the mesh frame.

41.heading: Step 8: Pulling the Paper Sheet
41.text:
Step 8: Pulling the Paper Sheet
We fill a wide tub (a vat) with water and pour in our
blended paper pulp, mixing it thoroughly so the fibers
are suspended evenly. We then take our homemade
wooden mesh, submerge it completely under the water
at an angle, level it out, and slowly lift it straight up. As
the water drains freely through the cloth mesh, a
beautiful, uniform layer of interwoven wet paper fibers
is left resting on the surface.

PULLING THE
SHEET
Fig 8: Lifting fibers from the vat.
4. Phase C: Seed Integration and Finishing
Step 9: Pressing the Mustard Seeds
While the newly formed paper sheet is still highly
saturated and resting on the cloth mesh, we carefully
scatter dry mustard seeds evenly across the surface. We
selected mustard seeds because they are small enough
to sit flat within thin paper, possess a durable outer
shell that resists rotting during the wet phase, and have
a highly reliable germination rate. Using our fingers, we
gently press the mustard seeds down into the soft pulp
so they become locked inside the fibers without being
crushed.

SEED
INTEGRATION
Fig 9: Adding viable mustard seeds.

42.heading: Step 10: Pressing and Air Drying
42.text:
Step 10: Pressing and Air Drying
Finally, we use a dry sponge to gently press the
underside of the cloth mesh, using capillary action to
absorb excess dripping water. We then carefully invert
the wet sheet onto a flat, dry towel or board. The sheets
are placed in a warm, well-ventilated room to air-dry
naturally. Avoiding high heat is critical, as extreme
temperatures would kill the seeds. Once all moisture
has evaporated, we have strong, fully functional seed
paper ready for testing.
☀
CONTROLLED
DRYING
Fig 10: Evaporating moisture safely.
5. Next Steps: Testing & Evaluation Phase
The physical creation of the paper is only the first half of our project. To satisfy the requirements for
Phase 3 (Project Testing and Evaluation), our upcoming work will focus on rigorous quantitative
analysis:
P h y s i c a l   Q u a l i t y   T e s t i n g :  We will examine the final dried sheets for structural
integrity, tensile strength, thickness consistency, and suitability for writing.
C o n t r o l l e d   P l a n t i n g   E x p e r i m e n t :  We will plant samples of our mustard seed paper
under controlled soil and light conditions (Group B). Simultaneously, we will plant
bare mustard seeds directly into the soil to act as our baseline control (Group A).
D a t a   C o l l e c t i o n   &   A n a l y s i s :  We will monitor the test pots daily, recording the days
until emergence (germination time), overall germination percentage, and early seedling
height. Comparing Group A and Group B will allow us to scientifically evaluate the
viability of turning university waste into a sustainable agricultural product.

Section 1: Executive Summary & Scientific Foundation
Every  day,  academic  institutions  generate  large  volumes  of  discarded  paper  from  classroom
assignments,  examination  sheets,  office  circulars,  notebook  pages,  and  cardboard  packaging.
Conventional paper recycling recovers cellulose fibers for industrial reuse, but the process requires
heavy chemical de-inking, bleaching, and high energy input, and the resulting paper is eventually
discarded again. Our project at IUST Awantipora investigates a circular, zero-waste alternative:
converting campus paper waste directly into biodegradable, plantable seed paper embedded with
mustard seeds.
To succeed in the Phase 2 Implementation Evaluation (40 points) and Phase 3 Testing Evaluation (30
points), it is not enough to simply make handmade paper as a craft activity. Evaluators look for
scientific understanding: why different papers break down at different speeds in water, how printer
toner and pen inks affect germinating seeds, what happens when we mix different paper types
together, and how we test seed viability in the laboratory using standard Petri dish filter paper
methods.
This compendium provides the complete theoretical and experimental knowledge base for our project
in clear, simple language. It covers the chemistry of seven distinct paper types, five categories of
writing  and  printing  inks,  an  exhaustive  matrix  of  paper-and-ink  combinations,  the  official
International Seed Testing Association (ISTA) Whatman filter paper method, detailed examples of
seed paper production across India and the world, and a complete defense guide for answering panel
questions.
Key Scientific Finding Supporting Our Project:  A peer-reviewed study by  Emperador et al.
(2024)  tested vegetable seeds in recycled paper versus control soil and proved that  mustard seeds
achieved a 96.30% germination rate in recycled paper —identical to their 96.30%
germination rate in natural soil (P = 0.057, no statistically significant loss of viability). This directly
validates our team's choice of mustard seeds as the ideal model crop for campus waste seed paper.

56.heading: Section 2: What Paper Is Made Of (Simple Fiber Science)
56.text:
Section 2: What Paper Is Made Of (Simple Fiber Science)
To explain to evaluators why some papers dissolve quickly in a water bucket while others stay stiff for
hours, we first need to understand the four basic ingredients inside commercial paper:
Cellulose Fibers (The Skeleton):  Paper is made of microscopic plant tubes called cellulose
fibers, usually extracted from wood, cotton, or recycled agricultural waste. Long fibers (like in
brown cardboard) make strong, tear-resistant paper. Short fibers (like in egg trays or newspaper)
make soft, crumbly paper that absorbs water very fast.
Hydrogen Bonds (The Natural Magnet):  When wet cellulose fibers are pressed together and
dried on a mesh, the oxygen and hydrogen atoms on neighboring fibers lock together
automatically. These are called hydrogen bonds. When we soak paper in water, water molecules
slip between the fibers and unlock these bonds so the paper can be reshaped.
Sizing Agents (The Waterproof Glue):  If paper were made of pure cellulose, fountain pen
ink would spread out like a blotter towel. To stop ink from bleeding, paper factories add "sizing"
chemicals such as starch, rosin, or Alkyl Ketene Dimer (AKD). More sizing means water takes
much longer to soak into the paper.
Mineral Fillers (The White Powder):  White papers like A4 printer sheets and sketch pads
contain 10% to 25% powdered minerals—mainly Calcium Carbonate (chalk) and Kaolin (white
clay)—to make the page bright white, smooth, and heavy. When recycled into thick seed paper, too
much chalk filler can dry into a hard crust that blocks baby plant shoots.
Lignin (The Brown Wood Glue):  Unbleached brown cardboard contains natural lignin, the
stiff compound that holds tree bark and wood together. Lignin repels water initially during
soaking, but once broken down in soil, it turns into rich organic humus that feeds soil microbes.
Section 3: Complete Analysis of All Paper Types We Can Use
In our project, we collected and examined several types of waste paper around the IUST campus and
hostels, alongside laboratory reference papers. Below is the detailed breakdown of each paper type,
how fast it loosens in water, and whether it helps or harms seed germination.
3.1 Standard A4 Printer & Copier Paper
What it is:  Bleached wood-pulp paper (usually 70 to 80 GSM—grams per square meter) used in
university offices, photocopy shops, and computer labs for assignments and question papers.
How fast it loosens in water:  Medium speed (2 to 6 hours of soaking). Because A4 paper is
treated with starch sizing and packed with calcium carbonate chalk filler to survive hot laser printers,
water cannot penetrate the surface instantly. Tearing A4 sheets into narrow strips exposes the raw
inner fibers and cuts soaking time in half.
BS DYOD IUST Awantipora • Seed Paper Research & Viva Compendium (Sadiya, Gufran, Aatif) Page 2 of 23

57.subject: Paper Fiber Science & Plant Phytotoxicity
57.heading: Effect on seed growth:  Moderate (6/10 when used alone). Pure A4 pulp has short,
57.text:
Effect on seed growth:  Moderate (6/10 when used alone). Pure A4 pulp has short, fine fibers and
chalk dust that pack very tightly together as the sheet dries. If a pure A4 seed paper sheet dries out
even slightly in the soil pot, it forms a stiff, cement-like crust that traps the delicate mustard shoot
underneath. Additionally, calcium carbonate makes the pulp slightly alkaline (pH 7.8 to 8.5). A4
paper works best when mixed with coarser papers like cardboard or egg trays.
3.2 Ruled Notebook & Lined Examination Test Papers
What it is:  Lighter bleached wood or agro-residue paper (55 to 65 GSM) used in student notebooks
and university answer scripts.
How fast it loosens in water:  Moderately fast (1 to 3 hours). Notebook paper is thinner and has
less surface glue than A4 printer paper, so water softens it much faster in the bucket.
Effect on seed growth:  Good (7/10). Because it is thinner and contains less mineral chalk than
heavy A4 copier paper, notebook pulp forms softer sheets that tear open easily when the mustard
seed swells and sends out its first root (radicle).
3.3 Corrugated Cardboard Waste
What it is:  Unbleached brown packaging boxes made of two flat linerboards and a wavy middle
layer (fluting), held together by natural cornstarch glue.
How fast it loosens in water:  Slowest (12 to 24 hours). Cardboard is thick, heavily compressed,
and contains natural wood lignin that resists water at first. However, once water penetrates the wavy
air channels and dissolves the cornstarch glue, the layers peel apart easily by hand.
Effect on seed growth:  Very Good (8/10). Cardboard has long, coarse, unbleached pine fibers and
zero chemical bleach or chalk filler. When formed into a sheet, these rough fibers cross over each
other like tiny logs, leaving microscopic air tunnels (high porosity). These air spaces hold moisture
like a sponge and allow oxygen to reach the seed, while giving the root easy gaps to push through.
3.4 Sketchbook, Drawing & Chart Paper
What it is:  Heavyweight cartridge or chart paper (120 to 200 GSM) used by design and architecture
students for sketching, posters, and watercolour work.
How fast it loosens in water:  Slow (6 to 12 hours). Sketch paper is specifically engineered not to
buckle or dissolve when wet paint or ink is applied. It contains heavy internal and surface sizing
(starch, gelatin, or synthetic polymers) and is tightly pressed under heavy steel rollers at the factory.
Effect on seed growth:  Poor when used alone (4/10). When blended and dried, sketch paper pulp
re-bonds into a dense, leather-like sheet with very low permeability. Water takes a long time to soak
through it in the soil, and germinating mustard seedlings often struggle to pierce the tough fiber mat,
causing the shoot to bend sideways (etiolation) or rot underneath. It should only be used in small
proportions (10% to 20%) to add strength to weak pulps.
BS DYOD IUST Awantipora • Seed Paper Research & Viva Compendium (Sadiya, Gufran, Aatif) Page 3 of 23

58.documentTitle: BS DYOD Term-End Project Literature & Technical Compendium: Waste Paper to Seed Paper
58.subject: Paper Fiber Science & Plant Phytotoxicity
58.heading: 3.5 Molded Pulp Egg Trays & Fruit Cartons
58.text:
3.5 Molded Pulp Egg Trays & Fruit Cartons
What it is:  Rough grey or brown trays used to pack eggs and apples, manufactured from 100%
recycled newsprint and cardboard slurry without any surface coating or sizing glue.
How fast it loosens in water:  Fast (15 to 30 minutes). Because egg trays have already been pulped
once and contain zero waterproofing glue, they drink up water immediately like a dry sponge and fall
apart into soft mush with simple hand squeezing.
Effect on seed growth:  Excellent (9/10). Egg tray pulp is one of the best materials in the world for
seed paper. Its short, fluffy fibers create a soft, breathable, crumbly blanket around the mustard seed.
It retains up to 4 times its weight in water and offers almost zero physical resistance to the emerging
root and shoot.
3.6 Laboratory Filter Paper (Whatman Filter Paper)
What it is:  Pure alpha-cellulose paper made from 100% high-grade cotton linters, completely free of
wood lignin, starch glue, chalk fillers, or optical brighteners  Cytiva (2020) .
How fast it loosens in water:  Very Fast (5 to 15 minutes). With zero sizing chemicals and a pure
porous network, water wicks into filter paper within seconds (rising at least 30 mm vertically in 2
minutes according to  ISTA (2018)  standards).
Effect on seed growth:  Gold Standard (10/10). Because it is chemically neutral (pH 6.5 to 7.0),
free of any toxic salt ions (low electrical conductivity), and holds an ideal balance of water and air,
Whatman filter paper is the official benchmark medium used in biology laboratories worldwide to
test seed germination inside Petri dishes.
3.7 Newspaper & Tissue Paper
What it is:  Lightweight mechanical wood pulp (newspaper, 45 GSM) or crêped sanitary cellulose
(tissue, 15 to 25 GSM).
How fast it loosens in water:  Instant to Fast (2 to 20 minutes). Tissue disintegrates in seconds;
newspaper softens in 15 minutes.
Effect on seed growth:  Good (7.5/10). Very soft for roots, though pure tissue pulp makes sheets
that are too weak and fragile to handle unless mixed with stronger A4 or cardboard fibers. Most
modern newspapers use soy-based or vegetable-oil inks, which are safe for soil microbes.

Section 4: Deep Dive into Ink Chemistry & Effect on Seed Growth
During our mentor discussion, a central question was raised:  What exact effect does ink have on the
paper pulp and on the germinating seeds?  Since campus waste paper contains printed question
papers, photocopied notes, and student handwriting in ballpoint, gel, and liquid pens, understanding
ink chemistry is essential for our evaluation.
4.1 Un-Inked Paper vs. Inked Paper: The Fundamental Difference
Un-inked paper  (such as clean A4 trimmings, blank notebook margins, and unprinted cardboard)
contains only cellulose fibers, natural starch, and calcium carbonate. It introduces zero synthetic
dyes, solvents, or polymers into the pulp vat. When planted, un-inked pulp has a clean white or
natural brown color and zero chemical phytotoxicity (plant poisoning).
Inked paper  introduces pigments, dyes, carrier solvents, and binder resins into the soaking bucket.
Whether an ink harms seed growth depends on two scientific factors:  (1) Water Solubility  (does
the ink dissolve into the water that the seed drinks during germination?) and  (2) Surface Coverage
Percentage  (is the page 5% covered in normal text, or 60% covered in solid black photographs?).
4.2 Laser Printer & Photocopier Toner (Dry Plastic Powder Ink)
What it is made of:  Many people assume printer ink is a liquid, but laser printers and university
photocopiers do not use liquid ink. They use  toner , which is an ultra-fine dry powder made of  85%
to 90% plastic polymer resin  (usually styrene-acrylate or polyester plastic) mixed with  Carbon
Black  (pure soot pigment) and tiny particles of  Iron Oxide  (magnetite). During printing, a heated
roller melts this plastic powder onto the A4 paper fibers at 180°C.

60.heading: What happens in the soaking bucket & blender:  Because laser toner is melted pla
60.text:
What happens in the soaking bucket & blender:  Because laser toner is melted plastic, it is
completely insoluble in water . It does not bleed or turn the water black. Instead, when we blend
printed exam papers, the mechanical blades shatter the melted toner into microscopic black specks
that float among the white fibers, turning the final seed paper a speckled light grey.
Effect on seed growth:
Normal Text Pages (5% to 15% toner coverage):  Safe for germination. Because the solid
carbon-plastic specks cannot dissolve in water, they cannot pass through the semi-permeable cell
membranes of the mustard seed root. The seed germinates normally (90% to 96% germination).
Heavily Printed Pages (>40% solid black graphics/diagrams):  Harmful and should be
rejected during sorting. High amounts of hydrophobic (water-repelling) plastic toner coat the
cellulose fibers, preventing the seed paper from absorbing water evenly. Furthermore, putting
large quantities of synthetic styrene-acrylate polymer into soil introduces non-biodegradable
microplastics.
4.3 Inkjet Printer Ink (Liquid Office & Home Printers)
What it is made of:  Inkjet printers spray microscopic droplets of liquid ink made of water (60% to
80%), humectants like ethylene glycol or diethylene glycol (to stop the printhead from drying out),
surfactants, and organic dyes or pigments.
What happens in the soaking bucket:  Water-based inkjet dyes dissolve rapidly into the soaking
water, tinting the water pastel blue, pink, or grey.
Effect on seed growth:  Safe in normal quantities, provided the soaking water is drained and
replaced with fresh water before sheet formation. Modern inkjet inks are manufactured without toxic
heavy metals (no lead, mercury, or cadmium). However, if concentrated glycol solvents from heavily
colored pages are left in the pulp water without rinsing, they can slightly increase the osmotic
pressure of the water, slowing down initial seed water uptake by 12 to 24 hours.
4.4 Ballpoint Pen Ink (Oil-Based Paste Ink)
What it is made of:  Standard blue, black, and red ballpoint pens (used on most student test
papers) contain a thick, high-viscosity paste made of  25% to 40% dyes  dissolved in  oil-based
organic solvents  (such as benzyl alcohol or phenoxyethanol) and synthetic resins (alkyd or
phenolic resin).
What happens in the soaking bucket:  Because oil and water do not mix, ballpoint pen ink is
hydrophobic. When you soak a handwritten test paper in a bucket of water, the blue ballpoint writing
stays firmly stuck to the paper fibers and barely bleeds into the water at all. When blended, the dyed
fibers mix evenly into the pulp.

61.text:
Effect on seed growth:  Minimal to Zero negative effect on normal handwritten pages. Why? First,
handwritten notes cover less than 3% to 5% of the total surface area of a sheet of paper. Second, the
volatile alcohol solvent (benzyl alcohol) evaporates completely within minutes of the student writing
on the page—months before we collect the paper! Third, because the remaining dye-resin paste is
locked onto the fibers and does not dissolve into the water, the germinating mustard seed does not
absorb it.
4.5 Gel Pen Ink (Water-Based Biopolymer Gel)
What it is made of:  Gel pens use solid pigment particles (like copper phthalocyanine for blue or
iron oxide/carbon black) suspended in water thickened with a natural biopolymer gel called  xanthan
gum  (made by fermenting simple sugars) and polyacrylate thickeners.
What happens in the soaking bucket:  Gel ink softens in water and releases tiny pigment
particles without releasing toxic solvents.
Effect on seed growth:  Very Safe. Xanthan gum is a natural, biodegradable polysaccharide that
actually holds moisture around the seed, and the trace pigment levels on handwritten notes are non-
toxic to plant roots.
4.6 Liquid Ink Pens (Pilot V5/V7, Rollerball & Fountain Pens)
What it is made of:  Liquid ink pens use pure, low-viscosity water-based solutions containing 90%
water, a small amount of glycerol, and water-soluble acid or direct dyes (such as Acid Blue 93 or
Direct Black).
What happens in the soaking bucket:  The moment a page written with a Pilot pen or fountain
pen touches water in the bucket, the ink bleeds out into the water like a cloud of blue or black dye.
Effect on seed growth:  Safe—and easiest to clean! Because liquid pen ink is 100% water-soluble,
70% to 85% of the ink washes out into the soaking bucket water  during our 12-to-24-hour
hydration phase. When we pour off that dirty blue soaking water and blend the paper in fresh clean
water, almost all the dye is already gone! If we did not drain the dirty soaking water, high
concentrations of aniline/acid dyes could stain the seed coat and slightly reduce root hair elongation.

62.heading: 1.  Osmotic Stress (Salt & Solute Imbalance):  A dry seed absorbs water by a phy
62.text:
1.  Osmotic Stress (Salt & Solute Imbalance):  A dry seed absorbs water by a physical process
called  imbibition  and  osmosis —water naturally moves from an area of low dissolved salts (clean
water) into the seed (high internal solutes). If paper pulp water has high Electrical Conductivity
(EC) from dissolved ink salts, bleaching chlorides, or chemical sizing, it creates osmotic resistance,
making it harder for the seed to drink water and delaying germination.
2.  pH Shift (Alkaline or Acidic Shock):  Mustard seeds germinate best at a slightly acidic to
neutral pH of  6.0 to 7.0 . Heavily bleached A4 paper with high calcium carbonate filler pushes pH
up to 8.4 (alkaline), while certain industrial paper effluents drop pH to 5.4 (acidic). Extreme pH
slows down the natural enzymes (like amylase and protease) inside the seed that unlock stored
food for the embryo.
3.  Radicle Tip Inhibition & Chlorophyll Reduction:  Studies on paper effluent show that while
low dilutions (20% to 25%) allow normal or even stimulated seedling growth, 100% concentrated
chemical sludge reduces early root (radicle) length and decreases Chlorophyll-a and Chlorophyll-b
synthesis in the first green leaves (cotyledons)  Environment and Ecology (2025) .

Section 5: Complete Paper & Ink Combination Matrix (All
Combinations Explained)
One of the smartest questions an evaluator or mentor can ask is:  "What happens if you don't just use
one  type  of  paper,  but  combine  different  paper  types  and  inked  papers  together?"  In Materials
Science, combining two materials with opposite properties creates a  composite material  that is
better than either material alone. Below is the complete scientific analysis of every single combination
we can make from our collected samples.
5.1 Combination 1: A4 Printer-Inked Paper + Corrugated Cardboard (50:50 Mix)
Why combine them:  A4 printer paper has short, tight fibers and chalk that dry into a hard crust,
whereas corrugated cardboard has long, coarse, unbleached fibers with wide air gaps.
Physical sheet quality:  Produces a strong, medium-thick, earthy light-brown sheet with tiny grey
flecks from the printer toner. Very easy to lift off the cloth mesh without tearing.
Effect on seed growth:   Excellent (90% to 95% expected germination).   The  coarse
cardboard fibers act as "spacers" between the fine A4 fibers, completely preventing the A4 paper from
forming a hard crust. Water soaks in quickly through the cardboard channels, and the mustard root
pushes out effortlessly.
5.2 Combination 2: A4 Pen-Inked Notes + Corrugated Cardboard (50:50 Mix)
Why combine them:  Student lecture notes and test papers written with ballpoint or Pilot pens are
thinner than copier paper and contain zero plastic laser toner.
Physical sheet quality:  A soft, warm beige sheet with high flexibility and a natural handmade look.
Effect on seed growth:   Superior (93% to 96% expected germination).  Because Pilot pen ink
washes out during soaking and ballpoint ink covers less than 5% of the page, there is no plastic toner
barrier. Combined with the airy structure of cardboard, this is one of the best campus-waste
formulations possible.
5.3 Combination 3: A4 Inked Paper + Sketch/Chart Paper with Pen/Marker Ink
(50:50 Mix)
Why combine them:  Both materials are abundant in design and university classrooms.
Physical sheet quality:  Produces a very smooth, bright, stiff, card-like sheet that looks like
commercial greeting card stock and is very easy to write on with a pen.
Effect on seed growth:   Poor (55% to 70% expected germination; delayed by 2 to 4 days).
This is a "bad combination" for plant growth that we should highlight to evaluators as a negative
control! Both A4 paper and sketch paper are loaded with starch sizing and mineral fillers. When
combined, they lock together into a dense, low-porosity barrier. Even when the mustard seed
germinates underneath, the tender shoot struggles to pierce the wet card unless we prick tiny
pinholes in the sheet before planting.

5.4 Combination 4: A4 Inked Paper + Egg Tray Pulp (50:50 Mix)
Why combine them:  Egg tray pulp holds massive amounts of water and stays fluffy, while A4
fibers give the sheet flat strength and a smoother surface for pressing seeds.
Physical sheet quality:  Soft, slightly textured off-white or light grey sheet with moderate tear
strength.
Effect on seed growth:   Outstanding (95% to 98% expected germination).  The egg tray
fibers act as micro-sponges right next to the mustard seed coat, keeping moisture constant for 72
hours while the A4 fibers hold the sheet intact during handling.
5.5 Combination 5: A4 Inked Paper + Whatman Filter Paper (50:50 Mix)
Why combine them:  Mixing pure laboratory cotton cellulose with ordinary campus waste paper
dilutes the chalk fillers and sizing chemicals by 50%.
Physical sheet quality:  Crisp, bright, soft white sheet with rapid capillary water absorption.
Effect on seed growth:   Excellent (94% to 97% expected germination).  The pure filter paper
fibers wick water straight to the mustard seed within seconds of watering.
5.6 Combination 6: Corrugated Cardboard + Sketch/Chart Paper (70:30 or
50:50 Mix)
Why combine them:  If we want to recycle stiff sketch/chart waste without suffocating the seeds,
mixing it with coarse cardboard opens up the dense structure of the sketch paper.
Physical sheet quality:  Heavy, rigid board suitable for plantable gift tags, coasters, or notebook
covers.
Effect on seed growth:   Moderate to Good (75% to 85% expected germination).  The rough
cardboard fibers disrupt the continuous starch film of the sketch paper, creating weak spots where
mustard roots and shoots can break through.
5.7 Combination 7: Corrugated Cardboard + Egg Tray Pulp (50:50 Mix)
Why combine them:  Combining long unbleached fibers (cardboard) with short un-sized recycled
fibers (egg tray) creates a 100% unbleached, chemical-free agricultural mat.
Physical sheet quality:  Earthy brown, thick, spongy, and rough—not ideal for fine handwriting,
but perfect as a biodegradable "seed mat" or plantable pot liner.
Effect on seed growth:   Best Soil Performance (96% to 99% expected germination).  Zero
bleach, zero chalk, high aeration, and rapid biodegradation in soil by natural cellulase-producing
fungi.

Section 6: The "Watch Paper" Mystery Solved: Whatman Filter
Paper & Petri Dish Standard Protocol
During our meeting, our mentor mentioned testing seeds on "watch paper" inside a Petri dish. In
laboratory terminology, this refers to  Whatman Filter Paper  (which phonetically sounds like
"watch-man paper") used inside a  9-cm Glass Petri Dish  or covered  Watch Glass . This is the
official international standard method defined by the  International Seed Testing Association
(ISTA)  for testing both seed viability and paper toxicity  Cytiva (2020) ,  ISTA (2018) .
6.1 Why Scientists Use Whatman Filter Paper in a Petri Dish Instead of Soil
When we plant seed paper in garden soil, many outside variables can ruin the experiment: soil might
contain fungal spores, insects, uneven fertilizer pockets, or clay lumps. By testing our seeds and our
recycled paper inside a closed glass Petri dish lined with Whatman No. 1 Filter Paper, we create a
100% sterile, transparent, controlled micro-climate  where:
We can see the exact hour the tiny white root tip (radicle) breaks out of the mustard seed coat
without digging up soil!
Moisture does not evaporate quickly because the glass Petri dish lid traps humidity.
Whatman Grade 1 (Product Code 1001090) and Grade 181/3644 papers are made of 100% pure
cotton linters with neutral pH and zero toxic ions, providing a perfect 100% baseline to compare
our recycled waste papers against  Cytiva (2020) ,  ICRISAT (2020) .
6.2 Step-by-Step Lab Protocol: The ISTA "Top of Paper" (TP) Petri Dish Test
We can run this exact experiment in the IUST laboratory (or even in our hostel/home using clean
dishes) in just 5 days to generate gold-standard scientific graphs for our Phase 2 and Phase 3
presentations  ICRISAT (2020) :

1.  Prepare 4 Petri Dishes (9 cm diameter):  Wash and dry four clear glass Petri dishes and
label their lids with a marker:
Dish A (Laboratory Gold Control):  Lined with two circles of pure  Whatman No. 1
Filter Paper  + 25 bare mustard seeds placed on top.
Dish B (Pure A4 Inked Seed Paper):  A 9-cm circle cut from our recycled  A4 Inked Seed
Paper  containing 25 mustard seeds.
Dish C (Cardboard / Tri-Blend Seed Paper):  A 9-cm circle cut from our  A4 +
Cardboard Seed Paper  containing 25 mustard seeds.
Dish D (Soil Control):  A small dish/pot filled with standard garden soil + 25 bare mustard
seeds.
2.  Add Exact Measured Water:  Using a syringe or dropper, add exactly  4 mL to 5 mL of
distilled or clean boiled water  to each Petri dish so the paper is thoroughly moistened but
seeds are not swimming underwater (seeds need oxygen to breathe!).
3.  Incubation & Daily Observation:  Cover the Petri dishes with their glass lids and keep them at
room temperature (18°C to 22°C indoors) near indirect daylight.
4.  Counting Germination Every 12 to 24 Hours:  According to  ICRISAT (2020)  and  ISTA
(2018)  rules, a seed is officially counted as  germinated when the white radicle (root tip)
protrudes by 2 mm to 4 mm  through the seed coat and paper layer.
5.  Measuring Paper Capillary Quality (The 2-Minute Strip Test):  Cut a 10-mm wide vertical
strip of each handmade paper (A4, Cardboard blend, Sketch blend) and dip the bottom 20 mm
into a beaker of water. Measure how many millimeters the water climbs up the paper in 2
minutes. High-quality germination paper rises at least  30 mm in 2 minutes   ICRISAT (2020) !
Section 7: Where Seed Paper Is Made & Used in India (Detailed
National Map)
Our mentor and evaluators will certainly ask:  "Is  seed  paper  actually  made  in  India?  Which
institutes, cities, and startups are doing it, and how does our project compare?"  India is actually one

what commercial Indian companies do (using factory cotton rags) and what our IUST project does

Commission (KVIC), Ministry of MSME, Government of India , and is officially recognized

Organization:   21Fools  (based in Mumbai) is one of India's best-known sustainable stationery
social enterprises  21Fools (2024) .
What they did:  In August 2018, inspired by a tweet from industrialist Anand Mahindra about
Japan's green newspaper, 21Fools launched  India's first newspaper printed on plantable seed
paper   21Fools (2018) . They highlighted a critical statistic:  India's paper recovery and
recycling rate is only about 26% , meaning 74% of paper is wasted  21Fools (2018) . They
manufacture  Beej Kapas  (seed cotton) paper in thicknesses from 100 GSM to 350 GSM using pre-
consumer cotton waste from garment factories, embedding 15 to 20 varieties of seeds including Holy
Basil ( Tulsi ), Marigold, Tomato, Green Chilli, and Wildflowers  21Fools (2024) .
7.3 New Delhi / NCR: bioQ Eco Solutions & Wildlense
Organization:   bioQ  (New Delhi) produces mass-scale plantable seed paper stationery for corporate
events, schools, and government functions across India  bioQ (2024) .
What they do:  They convert cotton textile waste into plantable bookmarks, wedding invitations,
B6/A5 notebook covers, plantable children's coloring books, and  Tricolour Plantable Seed Paper
Badges  worn on Independence Day and Republic Day so that flags and badges are planted in pots
instead of thrown in dustbins after the ceremony  bioQ (2024) . They print exclusively on one side
using eco-friendly  water-based inks  to protect seed germination.

Organization:  Rural collectives like the  Gram Art Project  in Paradsinga (Madhya Pradesh /
Maharashtra border) work with rural women and small farmers to create zero-chemical handmade
seed papers, plantable festival  Rakhis , and seed balls using local farm residues, non-GMO native

7.6 Local Connection: Jammu & Kashmir's Heritage of  K o s h u r   K a g a z  & Why
Mustard Fits Kashmir
Bringing our project home to  IUST Awantipora and Jammu & Kashmir  gives us two powerful
points that will deeply impress evaluators:
Reviving Kashmir's 600-Year-Old Handmade Paper Heritage:  In the 15th century,
Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin (Budshah)  brought master papermakers from Samarkand to Kashmir,
establishing the famous  Kagazgari  industry in Nowshera and Phulwari (Srinagar). Traditional
Kashmiri handmade paper ( Koshur Kagaz ) was made by pulping waste cotton rags and hemp
fibers on floating wooden moulds, prized across India and Persia for its durability and
smoothness. Our project at IUST modernizes this historic Kashmiri craft by turning campus waste
paper into living, plantable seed paper!
Why Mustard ( T i l g o g u l   /   S a r s o o n ) is the Ideal Crop for Kashmir in November:
Commercial Indian seed paper from Mumbai or Delhi contains basil ( Tulsi ) or tomato seeds,
which require warm tropical temperatures (25°C to 30°C) and die in Kashmir's cold
November/December weather! In contrast,  Mustard ( B r a s s i c a   c a m p e s t r i s   /   B r a s s i c a
j u n c e a , locally called  T i l g o g u l ) is Kashmir's primary winter Rabi oilseed crop , sown
across Pulwama, Awantipora, and Anantnag right in October and November! Mustard seeds
naturally germinate at cool temperatures (10°C to 20°C), making our seed paper scientifically
adapted to the Kashmir Valley climate.
How Our IUST Project Differs from Commercial Indian Seed Paper:  Most commercial
Indian seed paper companies (like 21Fools and bioQ) use  pre-consumer white cotton cloth scraps
from textile mills  21Fools (2024) ,  bioQ (2024) . While tree-free, that does not solve the massive
problem of  post-consumer written and printed paper waste  piling up in universities. Our project
specifically tackles real, inked post-consumer university paper and cardboard waste and proves how
to turn it into viable plantable paper.

(Whatman grades) were codified for agricultural testing laboratories  ISTA (2018) .

Pioneers  Heidi Reimer-Epp and Mary Reimer  founded  Botanical PaperWorks  in Winnipeg,

Section 9: Practical Scientific Innovations We Can Introduce in
Our Project
Phase 1 and Phase 2 evaluations explicitly award points for  Innovation, Problem-Solving, and
Technical Competence . Here are five simple, low-cost scientific innovations our team can apply
and explain during the presentation:
9.1 Innovation 1: The "Two-Stage Pre-Soak Wash" (Natural De-Inking Without
Chemicals)
Industrial paper mills use toxic caustic soda (sodium hydroxide), hydrogen peroxide, and flotation
surfactants to remove ink. Instead, we use a simple physical method: we soak our torn inked papers
in the blue bucket for 18 to 24 hours. During this soak, water-soluble pen dyes (Pilot/fountain pens),
surface dust, and excess starch sizing leach out into the water. Before putting the paper into the
blender, we  drain and discard this first dirty water  and refill with fresh clean water. This
removes up to 80% of soluble dyes and salts with zero chemical cost!

71.text:
9.2 Innovation 2: Surface-Pressed Embedding vs. Blender/Vat Mixing
Many amateur projects dump seeds into the pulp bucket, which causes two problems: (1) seeds sink
to the bottom of the bucket in water, resulting in uneven seed count per sheet, and (2) seeds get
buried too deep inside thick pulp, suffocating the shoot. In our methodology (Step 9), we pull a
uniform wet sheet on our wooden cloth mesh first, and then  count an exact number of dry
mustard seeds (e.g., 25 or 50 seeds per sheet) and press them gently into the top wet
surface . This guarantees exact scientific repeatability and ensures every seed can breathe and
emerge easily.
9.3 Innovation 3: The "Pin-Prick Micro-Perforation" Technique for Stiff Papers
When recycling stiff papers like A4 copier sheets or sketch paper, drying shrinks the fibers tightly
together. While the sheet is half-dry, using a clean needle or toothpick to make tiny  micro-
perforations (pinholes) around the embedded seeds  creates microscopic breathing vents and
weak lines in the cellulose mat, increasing seedling emergence speed by 30% to 40%!
9.4 Innovation 4: Natural Kashmiri Bio-Additives (Turmeric & Compost Tea)
One common problem when wet seed paper is kept in a damp pot or Petri dish for several days is
white mold (fungus) growing on the wet paper starch. Adding  half a teaspoon of pure turmeric
powder ( H a l d i )  to the pulp water not only dyes the seed paper a vibrant golden yellow, but
curcumin in turmeric is a proven natural antifungal agent that stops mold from attacking the
germinating mustard seeds! Similarly, wetting the planted paper with diluted vermicompost water
provides instant nitrogen and potassium once the root emerges.
9.5 Innovation 5: Zero-Cost Upcycled Wooden Mould & Deckle
Instead of buying expensive commercial papermaking screens, our team constructed a functional
mould frame using four wooden sticks and fine porous mesh cloth (Step 7). This proves that any
school or rural community in Kashmir can replicate our recycling model at near-zero cost.
Section 10: Mathematical Formulas & Experimental Data
Framework
To score maximum points in  Data Collection/Prototyping (Phase 2)  and  Data Analysis
(Phase 3) , our documentation must present exact mathematical equations used in seed physiology
research  IJASRM (2019) ,  ICRISAT (2020) ,  Emperador et al. (2024) :
1. Germination Percentage (GP %) = (Number of Seeds Germinated ÷ Total Number
of Seeds Tested) × 100
2. Mean Germination Time (MGT) = ∑ (n i  × d i ) ÷ N   [where n i  = seeds germinated
on day d i , and N = total germinated seeds]
3. Seedling Vigour Index (SVI) = Germination Percentage (%) × Mean Total
Seedling Length (Root + Shoot in cm)

73.text:
Section 11: Complete Viva-Voce & November 17 Defense Question
Bank (20 Questions & Simple Answers)
Evaluators often ask sharp, probing questions during Phase 2 and Phase 3 presentations to test
whether every team member (Sadiya, Gufran, and Aatif) truly understands the science or simply
copied a craft video. Memorize these simple, confident answers:
Q1: "You haven't finished growing the plants yet. Why should we give you good marks
on November 17?"
Answer:  "Sir/Ma'am, according to the official DYOD Evaluation Strategy, November 17 is Phase 2
(Project Implementation), while Phase 3 (Project Testing and Data Analysis) is scheduled for
December 22. For Phase 2, we have completed our campus waste collection, contaminant sorting,
material  categorization,  soaking  hydration  setup,  homemade  mould  engineering,  and  a
comprehensive literature and material science study on fiber types and ink phytotoxicity. Our
physical stage-by-stage samples and methodology are ready for inspection today."
Q2: "What is 'watch paper' in a Petri dish and why did your mentor tell you to study it?"
Answer:  "It is Whatman Filter Paper (Grade 1 or Grade 181), which is made of 100% pure cotton
cellulose with zero glue, bleach, or chemicals. In biology labs under International Seed Testing
Association (ISTA) rules, scientists place Whatman filter paper inside a glass Petri dish with 4 mL of
distilled water to test seeds. Our mentor guided us to use this as a pure laboratory control so we can
compare how seeds sprout on pure cellulose versus our recycled inked campus paper without soil
bacteria interfering."
Q3: "Which paper loosens fastest in water, which takes the longest, and why?"
Answer:  "Filter paper and egg trays loosen the fastest (in 5 to 30 minutes) because they have short
fibers and zero waterproofing glue (sizing). A4 and notebook papers take medium time (2 to 6 hours)
because factories add starch sizing and chalk filler so pen ink doesn't bleed. Sketch paper and
corrugated cardboard take the longest (6 to 24 hours) because sketch paper has heavy surface sizing
for wet paint, and cardboard has thick compressed layers and natural wood lignin."
Q4: "Is printer ink on old exam papers toxic to seeds? What is printer ink actually
made of?"
Answer:  "Laser printer and photocopier ink is actually dry toner—a powder made of styrene-acrylate
plastic polymer mixed with carbon black and iron oxide, melted onto the page. Because it is solid
plastic, it does not dissolve in water and cannot be absorbed by plant roots. On normal text pages
(under 15% coverage), it breaks into harmless grey specks and seeds germinate at 92% to 96%.
However, pages with heavy black pictures (>40% coverage) repel water and add microplastics, so we
sort those out."

74.text:
Q5: "What about student handwriting in ballpoint pens, gel pens, and Pilot liquid ink
pens?"
Answer:  "Handwriting covers less than 5% of a page's surface. Ballpoint ink is oil-based, so it stays
locked onto the paper fibers and doesn't leach into water. Gel pen ink uses xanthan gum, a natural
sugar biopolymer that is completely safe. Liquid ink pens like Pilot V5 use water-soluble dye that
bleeds into our soaking bucket—and when we drain that dirty soaking water before blending, 75% to
85% of the dye is washed away before it ever touches our seeds!"
Q6: "Why does pure A4 paper sometimes reduce seed growth even if it has no ink at
all?"
Answer:  "Because A4 paper contains 15% to 20% calcium carbonate (chalk) filler and fine bleached
fibers that pack together tightly when drying. If a pure A4 sheet dries out slightly in the pot, it forms a
stiff, cement-like crust that physically blocks the tiny shoot from pushing up, and the chalk raises the
pH above 8.0."
Q7: "How do you fix that A4 crust problem?"
Answer:  "By combining A4 paper in a 50:50 blend with corrugated cardboard or egg tray pulp! The
long, coarse cardboard fibers act as spacers that create microscopic air tunnels in the sheet, holding
moisture like a sponge and giving the mustard roots and shoots easy gaps to push through."
Q8: "What happens if you mix A4 paper with Sketch or Chart paper?"
Answer:  "That creates a very stiff, smooth card that is great for writing on, but poor for seed
germination. Because both A4 and sketch paper contain heavy starch sizing and tightly packed fibers,
the combined sheet absorbs water slowly and acts as a tough barrier that delays or traps seedlings."
Q9: "Why did you choose mustard seeds instead of flower seeds or tomato seeds?"
Answer:  "Three scientific reasons: First, mustard seeds are tiny (1 to 2 mm) and round, so they sit
flat inside thin paper without getting crushed. Second, a 2024 peer-reviewed study by Emperador et
al. proved that mustard seeds achieve a 96.30% germination rate on recycled paper. Third, here in
Kashmir during November, warm-weather seeds like basil or tomato die in the cold, whereas mustard
( Tilgogul / Sarsoon ) is Kashmir's native winter Rabi crop that germinates rapidly in 3 to 5 days even
in cool temperatures!"
Q10: "Why don't the mustard seeds sprout early while the wet paper is drying in your
room?"
Answer:  "For a mustard seed to break its coat and sprout, it needs continuous moisture for 36 to 48
hours. In our process, we only press dry mustard seeds onto the wet pulp at the very end (Step 9),
immediately sponge out the excess water, and air-dry the thin sheet within 12 to 24 hours. The water
evaporates before germination is triggered, keeping the seed safely dormant."
Q11: "Why must you air-dry the seed paper in the shade instead of using a hairdryer,
heater, or hot sun?"
Answer:  "A seed contains a living plant embryo made of delicate proteins and enzymes. Heating wet
seeds above 40°C to 45°C denatures their enzymes and cooks the embryo, killing the seed. Cool,
ventilated room air-drying preserves 100% seed viability."

75.text:
Q12: "Why did you tear the paper by hand in Step 4 instead of only cutting it with
scissors or a shredder?"
Answer:  "Sharp scissor blades slice straight across cellulose fibers, shortening them and leaving
smooth edges. Tearing wet or dry paper by hand pulls the fibers apart at their natural joints, creating
frayed, feathered ends (fibrillation) that interlock much more strongly when forming a new sheet."
Q13: "Where in India is handmade and seed paper produced, and how is your project
different?"
Answer:  "India's premier government research center is the Kumarappa National Handmade Paper
Institute  (KNHPI)  in  Sanganer,  Jaipur  (under  KVIC,  Ministry  of  MSME),  which  researches
germination papers and waste fibers. Major Indian startups include 21Fools in Mumbai (who made
India's first plantable newspaper), bioQ in New Delhi, and the Gram Art Project in Madhya
Pradesh/Maharashtra. However, commercial Indian companies mostly use clean factory cotton cloth
scraps, whereas our project recycles post-consumer written and printed university paper waste."
Q14: "Is there any historical connection between handmade paper and Kashmir?"
Answer:   "Yes!  In  the  15th  century,  Sultan  Zain-ul-Abidin  (Budshah)  introduced  handmade
papermaking ( Kagazgari ) to Kashmir from Samarkand. Traditional  Koshur  Kagaz  was made in
Nowshera, Srinagar from recycled cotton rags and hemp pulp. Our project connects Kashmir's
historic handmade paper heritage with modern campus sustainability."
Q15:  "Doesn't  using  an  electric  kitchen  blender  use  more  electricity  than  the
environmental value of the paper?"
Answer:  "Because we soak our torn paper strips in a water bucket for 12 to 24 hours first, the water
naturally breaks the hydrogen bonds between fibers. As a result, the blender only needs to run in
short pulses for 15 to 20 seconds per batch, consuming negligible electricity."
Q16: "What is the ideal thickness (GSM) for plantable seed paper?"
Answer:  "Between 120 GSM and 220 GSM (about 0.3 mm to 0.5 mm thick). If a sheet is thinner
than 100 GSM, the 1.5-mm mustard seeds fall out because the fiber layer is too thin to hold them. If it
is thicker than 300 GSM, the sheet becomes too heavy for baby shoots to push through."
Q17: "Why do you remove staples, plastic tape, and laminated covers in Step 2?"
Answer:  "Metal staples rust and destroy blender blades, while plastic tape and lamination films do
not dissolve in water. If blended, plastic turns into microplastics that contaminate the soil when the
paper is planted."
Q18: "What happens to the paper fibers in the soil after the mustard seed sprouts?"
Answer:  "Paper is 85% to 95% natural plant cellulose. Soil microorganisms—especially fungi like
Trichoderma  and bacteria along with earthworms—secrete cellulase enzymes that break the cellulose
down into simple glucose sugars and organic humus within 3 to 8 weeks, enriching the soil and
holding moisture around the roots."
